!!⚠️ THE ONE PREFERENCE THAT FIGHTS ITSELF. «The thicker the better» for comfort, and the mattress thickness IS the cabinet depth - so every millimetre of comfort is taken directly out of the room's floor depth, in the room the bed stands in. Nobody has traded these against each other yet and the owner may not have connected them. !! THE VAULT ALREADY RECORDS THE FAILURE MODE: a real case chose the cabinet before the mattress and was left with 10 mm of clearance - so the mattress is fixed FIRST and the depth follows, never the reverse. The model can report, per candidate wall, how much floor depth each mattress thickness costs; the owner picks where to stop.

The open footprint plus a walking clearance on at least one long side decides whether the transformable zone works at all, and it fixes the SUPPORTING WALL - the single most irreversible item in DI-004. !! VERTICAL IS FEASIBLE ON HEIGHT: a 2000 mm mattress plus mechanism and plinth is roughly 2150-2250 against the 2500 mm CLEAR height, so the orientation can be chosen on layout grounds rather than forced by the ceiling. Horizontal would instead need ~2000 mm of uninterrupted wall LENGTH, which is the scarcer resource in this flat. !! The 2500 is clear height - screed top to ceiling underside - NOT the ~2550 slab-to-slab, which would silently add the slab thickness. !!⚠️ AND THE THING THAT MUST FIT IS THE CABINET, NOT THE MATTRESS. A wall-bed cabinet is wider than the mattress it holds - side panels, the lifting mechanism and its clearances - so comparing a mattress width against R7's 1750 clear span is comparing the wrong two numbers, which is the same mistake as comparing solid against clear. The CABINET EXTERNAL WIDTH is not recorded for any candidate bed and is a manufacturer figure. On 1750 clear: an 1800 mattress misses by 50 mm before the cabinet is even counted, so it is out; a 1600 mattress leaves 150 mm for two side panels and two fitting clearances, which is plausible but NOT yet demonstrated. Get the cabinet's external width from the maker before treating 1600 as settled.

!! SPECIFIED BY THE OWNER: a GLASS partition in FOUR or FIVE leaves that folds and retracts FULLY, so that when open it occupies only a small stack and the whole area reads as one living room for guests. !! THE REASON IT IS GLASS IS A STATED COMPROMISE, and it must not be silently optimised away: «I don't want to make the kitchen zone completely dark without natural light.» Glass buys daylight into the kitchen zone at the cost of sound and light isolation, and the owner has named that trade explicitly rather than assumed it away. !! STILL REQUIRED: the parked stack depth, which follows from leaf count and leaf width, and WHERE the stack parks - a leaf that folds into a doorway or against a radiator is a partition with nowhere to go.
!! REQUIRED INPUT. Seat-pull clearance behind a chair is the figure that decides whether the kitchen/living zone survives being closed off.
!! REQUIRED INPUT. The aisle must work in BOTH the open and the closed state of the partition, which is the constraint a single-state plan always misses.
